title: Mishima inlay on leather-hard clay
subtitle: Incised line decoration filled with contrasting slip before bisque firing
excerpt: Mishima is a Korean inlay technique: incised lines cut into leather-hard clay are filled with contrasting slip, then scraped back level to reveal crisp white or coloured lines on the body beneath. The technique requires the work to be kiln-fired. This tutorial covers the inlay process from incising through to the scraping-back stage, ready for bisque firing.
sourceNotes: Mishima technique derived from Korean Goryeo celadon inlay tradition (12th century); technique references derived from traditional inlay methodology and contemporary studio practice. Heritage attribution: 'mishima' is a Korean-into-Japanese term for the inlay practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: The drying stage where clay holds its shape but is still firm enough to cut clean lines without crumbling.
The first kiln firing, around cone 06, that hardens greenware into porous bisqueware.
A slip with a more glaze-like formulation, applied to clay for decorative effect.
A Korean inlay technique where incised lines in leather-hard clay are filled with contrasting slip, then scraped level to reveal crisp inlaid lines.

content.text: This technique requires kiln firing. The decorated piece must go through a bisque firing at cone 06 (approximately 1000°C) before glazing. Access to a studio kiln or community kiln is needed.
This technique works on thrown and hand-built forms. The carving must happen at the right
leather-hard
stage. If the clay is too soft, it smears. If it is too dry, it crumbles instead of cutting clean. A piece left at
leather-hard
for four to six hours at room temperature is usually ready.
What you need

A leather-hard clay piece: a slab, a hand-built panel, or a thrown bowl or tile. Porcelain-slip or coloured-slip-black in a small container. A fine liner brush and a needle tool or pointed carving tool. A metal rib or fettling knife for scraping back. A banding wheel is helpful for round pieces.
The inlay process
Draw or trace the design lightly onto the leather-hard surface with a pencil or needle tool. Keep lines simple:
mishima
reads well at 1 to 2 mm line width; finer than this and the slip will not fill reliably.

Incise each line with the needle tool or carving tool, cutting to a depth of 1 to 1.5 mm. Work in confident single passes rather than scrubbing back and forth: scrubbing raises clay burrs that will affect the scraping-back stage. The cut channel should have clean, vertical sides.

Blow away any clay crumbs from the incised lines. Brush away any remaining debris with a dry paintbrush: do not use a damp brush at this stage or it will wet the surface and make the slip adhesion weaker.
Apply
porcelain slip

over the incised design using a liner brush, loading enough slip to slightly overflow each line. Apply generously: the slip will shrink as it dries. Two or three passes over the same line ensures full coverage.

Leave the piece to dry until the slip has whitened and stiffened slightly: about 20 minutes. The slip must be firm enough not to smear when the rib touches it, but not so dry that it pulls away from the clay body at the cut edges.

Scrape back the excess slip with the metal rib or fettling knife held flat against the surface. Work across the design in a single steady pull rather than in short strokes: multiple passes build up parallel drag marks. The incised lines should appear as clean white (or coloured) inlaid strips against the red or grey clay body.

If the scraping leaves the surface rough, allow it to dry for a further 15 minutes and make a second scraping pass with a clean rib. Do not dampen the surface to smooth it: water will loosen the slip from the channels.
Allow the decorated piece to dry completely to
greenware
and
bisque fire
at cone 06. After bisque, the inlaid lines will appear as crisp contrasting marks. A clear or tinted glaze can then be applied over the bisqueware and fired to the body's mature temperature.
What it looks like when right

After scraping back, the incised lines should be filled to the level of the surrounding clay surface: the design reads as a flat inlay, not as raised lines or as grooves. The contrast should be clean: white slip against red earthenware or grey stoneware shows clearly as a pale line against a dark body. Under a celadon glaze, the white slip reads grey-white against the pale green glaze, as it does on the historical Korean originals.
Common mistakes
Incising too dry: the clay crumbles and the channel edges are ragged. Move the incising stage earlier in the leather-hard window.
Scraping too soon: the slip smears across the surface instead of coming away cleanly. Wait the full 20 minutes after applying the slip before scraping.

Slip shrinks away from channel edges after drying: the slip was too fluid when applied, or the clay body was too dry. Apply slip in two or three layers; keep the clay body at its prime leather-hard stage.

Inlay disappears under the glaze: the slip was not applied densely enough and the glaze colour dominated. Apply the slip in three layers minimum, and use a clear or celadon glaze that does not obscure light-coloured inlay.

rows.problem: Lines look fuzzy or double after scraping
rows.cause: Rib held at an angle rather than flat; multiple short scraping strokes instead of one long pull
rows.fix: Hold the rib flat against the surface. Make one long confident pull across the entire design in a single stroke.

rows.problem: Slip pulls away from the channel during firing
rows.cause: Different thermal contraction between slip and body; slip applied when the clay was too dry
rows.fix: Apply slip when the clay is at peak leather-hard (not dry leather-hard). Use a slip formulated to match the clay body's thermal contraction rate.
